questions.q: According to this lesson, why is trying to fix every visible problem immediately one of the most common new-governance-hire mistakes?
options: A new hire doesn't yet know which problems are already being worked on, which are politically sensitive, or what an "obvious fix" might break elsewhere
Because governance problems are never worth fixing at all
Because new hires are not allowed to speak in meetings during their first year
Because fixing problems quickly always damages a company's data
questions.explain: The lesson explains that a new hire lacks the organizational context to safely judge which changes are safe, which is why learning the landscape comes before making changes.

questions.q: What is the primary focus of days 1-30 in this lesson's 90-day plan?
options: Listening and mapping — meeting key people and reading what already exists before suggesting anything new
Proposing a complete overhaul of the classification scheme
Taking over as the sole decision-maker for all data definitions
Avoiding all contact with data owners and stewards
questions.explain: Days 1-30 focus on learning the landscape: meeting stakeholders and understanding existing processes, not producing new work yet.

questions.q: What kind of work does this lesson recommend taking on during days 31-60?
options: A defined, scoped, low-risk piece of existing work, such as one dictionary entry or one glossary definition, reviewed through the existing approval process
A brand-new, broad initiative proposed entirely from scratch with no review
No work at all — days 31-60 should be spent only observing
Only work that bypasses the organization's existing review process
questions.explain: The second month is about scoped, low-risk contributions that build trust, reviewed through whatever approval process already exists.

questions.q: By days 61-90, what does this lesson recommend a new governance hire be ready to do?
options: Own something small end to end, such as running a review meeting or a classification decision, based on a pattern noticed in month two
Resign and look for a different role entirely
Hand off all responsibilities to someone more senior permanently
Avoid asking for feedback until a formal annual review
questions.explain: By the third month, the lesson recommends owning a small, complete piece of the governance process end to end, and asking for direct feedback at the 90-day mark.

questions.q: What makes a good "first small win," according to this lesson?
options: Something specific, visible, low-risk, and finished — like cleaning up one confusing glossary entry — rather than an ambitious, half-done overhaul
Redesigning the organization's entire classification scheme in the first week
A win that depends entirely on another team failing to do their job
A win that is never shared with anyone else in the organization
questions.explain: The lesson specifically contrasts a small, finished, visible win against an ambitious but half-done overhaul as the better choice early in a role.
